brief.intro: A residential building — this generic template applies whenever the schedule does not need to distinguish rise or unit type — is, once the structure is up, essentially won and lost in the finishing trades. The programme is a long, repeating chain of blockwork, waterproofing, tiling, MEP first and second fix, paint and joinery that moves unit after unit and floor after floor. Unlike an industrial or critical facility, there is no heavy plant or complex commissioning; the risk instead is coordination and sequence discipline — wet areas (bathrooms, kitchens) must be waterproofed and tested before tiling closes them in, and MEP first fix must be complete and inspected before walls are plastered or floors are screeded over it. Productivity in the finishing package is highly repetitive, so the programme is usually paced by how fast a fixed crew can move from unit to unit, not by any single long-lead item. The last phase — snagging, de-snagging and the unit handover pack — is often underestimated and deserves real time in the plan.

scope.name: Structure & shell
scope.desc: Frame/slab and blockwork & partitions built to receive the finishing trades.

scope.name: Waterproofing
scope.desc: Roof, wet areas (bathrooms, kitchens) and balconies waterproofed and tested before they are closed in.

scope.name: MEP first fix
scope.desc: Power, plumbing, drainage and data/ELV containment routed within walls and slab before plaster.

scope.name: Plaster / drywall & substrate
scope.desc: Wall and ceiling substrate preparation, and screed to receive flooring.

scope.name: Floor & wall tiling / stone
scope.desc: Wet areas and common finishes laid on the prepared screed.

scope.name: MEP second fix
scope.desc: Devices, fixtures and fittings connected and tested after the finishes are in.

scope.name: Sanitary fixtures & fittings
scope.desc: Baths, basins, WCs and kitchen fittings installed and tested.

scope.name: Testing, snagging & handover
scope.desc: Circuit and flush testing, snagging/de-snagging, and the unit handover pack.

the repeating sequence of trades that moves from one floor or unit to the next at a steady pace.

must_get_right: Wet-area waterproofing must be complete and tested before tiling closes it in — it's the most common and expensive rework if skipped or rushed.
MEP first fix must be inspected and signed off before plaster/screed covers it — buried defects are costly to trace and fix later.
The finishing trades move unit-by-unit or floor-by-floor at a steady, repeatable pace — plan and track it that way, not as one lump percentage.
Protect real time for snagging, de-snagging and the handover pack at the end — it is routinely compressed and becomes the actual bottleneck to handover.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Finishing trades are typically modelled as a repeating unit/floor cycle — a 'typical unit' duration replicated across identical units — rather than as fully discrete activities per unit. The network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones; total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Structure runs a 6-day week; finishing trades run 6-day, moving to two shifts near handover where needed to compress the unit cycle; testing and snagging are scheduled around inspection availability rather than a fixed calendar.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs structural slab readiness → blockwork/partitions → wet-area waterproofing (tested before tiling) → MEP first fix → plaster/screed → tiling → MEP second fix → paint → joinery & sanitary fixtures → snagging → handover. On multi-unit buildings, the critical path is usually the finishing-crew cycle time repeating unit to unit or floor to floor, not any single long-lead item.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design and finishes specification are frozen; structure is handed over floor-by-floor or unit-by-unit on a fixed cadence; wet-area waterproofing is tested before it is covered; a single finishing-crew mobilisation is sized to the target unit-cycle time.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: Residential has few true long-lead items compared to industrial or critical-facility types; the schedule-relevant materials and their typical lead times are:

rows: Before tiling front reaches each unit

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Finishing-crew availability and unit-to-unit handover discipline pace the programme; material laydown and vertical hoisting are constrained in a live construction building; wet trades must be sequenced so tiling never starts over uncured waterproofing; vertical access (hoists, stairs) is shared across trades and units.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: waterproofing failures and re-tests, finishing-crew productivity below plan slowing the unit cycle, and late joinery or fixture deliveries. Schedule contingency is held before snagging and handover rather than spread thinly across finishing activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
